text.p: The following are the main stories from Wednesday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Parliament agrees to abolish local capital trading tax on companies. Ruling coalition sticks to tax reform plans.
- Chancellor Helmut Kohl and President Roman Herzog praise solidarity of Germans during flood crisis.
- Ifo institute predicts German economic growth of 2.25 percent for 1997.
- Incoming orders rise 1.5 percent in June.
- Earnings improve in metal industry but not still far from satisfactory.
HANDELSBLATT
- Kohl's coalition agrees solidarity surcharge on income tax will be cut from January 1, 1998.
- Ifo says debates about tax reform and Europe's planned single currency are damaging Germany's economic prospects.
- Government pledges 500 million marks in aid for victims of flood in eastern Germany.
- U.S. dollar continues climb against deutschemark.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- Court rejects property claim by aristocratic family which says its fortune was seized by the Nazis.
- Jewish community leader calls on German banks to examine their role under the Nazis.
- IG Metall trade union leader Klaus Zwickel rejects return to 40-hour working week.
- Industrial orders and production both show substantial rises for first half of 1997.
DIE WELT
- Liberal Free Democrats (FDP) propose coalition with Social Democrats (SPD) in city-state of Hamburg after elections due later this year.
- Ifo institute experts view possible turning point in German labour market situation.
- Labour Minister Norbert Bluem hopes for compromise with opposition over reform of pensions system.
- Eastern German flood causes millions of marks in damage to local economy. Smaller firms are hit hardest.
